source_label: Huddleston & Pullum et al., The Cambridge Grammar of the English Language (Cambridge University Press, 2002): chapter and section structure only
assumptions: Every example sentence, analysis and explanation is original and authored for this page; none is reproduced from the book.
The analyses follow the framework and terminology of the book as known to the author; they have not yet been checked against the book's text, and the page is not endorsed by the authors or publisher.

Chapter and section references come from the publisher's contents pages. A concept cites only the chapter when its section could not be verified, and page numbers are section start pages only. All chapter page ranges were rechecked against Cambridge Core on 2026-10-01.

Inflection and word-formation (Chapters 18 and 19) are drawn as structures inside a single word, and punctuation (Chapter 20) as marks attached to constituent boundaries, not as parts of constituent trees. Antecedents are recorded as links, not branches.
Main-clause interrogatives with subject-auxiliary inversion are described in text but not drawn as trees in this version.
